howItWorks.intro: This calculator works backward from the same building blocks the ACA Marketplace uses to price coverage. It starts with a baseline Silver-tier monthly premium, scales it by an age factor that mirrors the ACA's allowed 3:1 age-rating curve, adjusts for the number of people in your household, then applies your chosen metal tier and an income-based subsidy estimate to land on a monthly and annual premium.

rules.name: Premium
rules.formula: Premium = Base × Age Factor × Family Size Factor - Subsidy
rules.explanation: Adjusted base premium minus any applicable subsidies.

howItWorks.outro: Real premiums are set by licensed insurers and vary by rating area, tobacco use, and the specific plan menu in your county — none of which this simplified calculator can see. Treat this as a rough planning estimate, not a real quote. Use it to get a feel for the range you're likely looking at, then confirm exact pricing and subsidy eligibility on HealthCare.gov, your state's Marketplace exchange, or with a licensed insurance agent before you enroll.

faq.question: Do I qualify for a Premium Tax Credit subsidy?
faq.answer: Likely, if your household income falls within the Marketplace's eligibility range for your household size and you don't have access to affordable employer coverage — the exact cutoff shifts with legislation, so check current-year rules. The credit is calculated on a sliding scale tied to your income as a percentage of the Federal Poverty Level; lower-income households pay a smaller share of the benchmark Silver plan's premium, with the credit covering the rest. This calculator's subsidy figure is only a rough estimate — actual eligibility and amount are determined by HealthCare.gov or your state Marketplace based on your real application.

faq.question: Why does the Silver tier matter more than the others for subsidies?
faq.answer: The Premium Tax Credit is benchmarked against the second-cheapest Silver plan available in your area, regardless of which tier you actually buy. Choose Bronze or Gold instead, and the same dollar credit still applies — you're just applying it against a different premium. Silver plans are also the only tier eligible for Cost-Sharing Reductions, which lower deductibles and copays for qualifying lower-income households, on top of the premium credit.

faq.question: Why would two people the same age pay different premiums?
faq.answer: Location and tobacco use, mainly — two factors this simplified calculator doesn't ask for. Insurers price plans by rating area (roughly your county or ZIP code), so identical coverage can cost noticeably more in a high-cost-of-living region. Most states also allow a tobacco surcharge of up to 50% for smokers. Household size and the specific insurer's plan menu add further variation.

faq.question: What's the actual difference between Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum?
faq.answer: The tiers describe actuarial value — the share of an average enrollee's medical costs the plan is designed to cover over a year: roughly 60% for Bronze, 70% for Silver, 80% for Gold, and 90% for Platinum. Premiums rise as actuarial value rises, while deductibles and out-of-pocket costs fall. A healthy household that rarely uses care often comes out ahead with a lower-premium Bronze or Silver plan; someone managing an ongoing condition may spend less overall with a higher-premium Gold or Platinum plan despite the higher monthly cost.

faq.question: Is this the premium I'll actually be charged?
faq.answer: No — treat it as a rough planning estimate, not a real quote. Actual premiums are set by licensed insurers and the ACA Marketplace based on your full application, your exact rating area, tobacco use, and the specific plan you select, and they can differ meaningfully from this estimate. Confirm real pricing and subsidy eligibility directly with HealthCare.gov or your state's Marketplace exchange before you enroll.

faq.question: What income figure should I enter?
faq.answer: Use your best estimate of Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) for the year you'll actually have coverage, not last year's tax return. Marketplace subsidies are trued up against your real income when you file taxes, so a significant mismatch between your estimate and your actual income can mean owing money back or receiving an additional credit at tax time.

howWeCalculate.intro: Under the hood, the calculator runs a few sequential adjustments rather than a single lookup table, so you can see roughly how each input pulls the result.
steps: Starts from a baseline monthly premium for a Silver-tier plan, the ACA's reference point for both pricing and subsidy calculations
Applies an age factor that scales the premium along a curve similar to the ACA's allowed 3:1 ratio between the oldest and youngest adult enrollees
Adjusts for household size, since ACA premiums are generally built by summing per-member costs rather than charging one flat family rate

Applies your selected metal tier — Bronze, Silver, Gold, or Platinum — to shift the premium relative to the Silver baseline, then estimates a Premium Tax Credit based on your income relative to the Federal Poverty Level for your household size
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This is a simplified planning estimate, not a real quote. Actual premiums are set by insurers and the ACA Marketplace based on your real application, rating area, and plan selection, and can differ substantially from this estimate — and subsidy eligibility should always be confirmed directly with HealthCare.gov or your state Marketplace, not assumed from this or any calculator.

whenToUse.intro: This calculator is built for the planning stage — before you're comparing real plan quotes — when you want a rough sense of what Marketplace coverage might cost at your age, income, and household size.
scenarios: Before open enrollment, to get a ballpark monthly premium and subsidy range across Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum before you start comparing real plans on HealthCare.gov
When your income is about to change — a raise, a new job, a dependent leaving your household — and you want to see roughly how that shifts your expected subsidy
When deciding whether a lower-premium Bronze plan or a subsidy-eligible Silver plan makes more sense given your household's expected medical usage
When comparing how premiums might differ for a spouse or dependent in a different age band, given ACA age-rating rules
When you want a sanity check against a quote you've already received, to see whether it's roughly in the range you'd expect

sections.title: What This Calculator Estimates
sections.body: The Health Insurance Premium Calculator gives you a directional read on what an ACA Marketplace health plan might cost, using four inputs: your annual income, your age, your household (family) size, and the metal tier you're considering — Bronze, Silver, Gold, or Platinum. Plug those in and it returns an estimated monthly premium, the annualized cost, and a rough Premium Tax Credit that could offset it. Under the Affordable Care Act, metal tiers describe actuarial value, not plan quality: a Bronze plan is designed to cover about 60% of the average enrollee's medical costs over a year, Silver about 70%, Gold about 80%, and Platinum about 90%, with the enrollee responsible for the remainder through deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. Lower actuarial value means a lower premium but higher out-of-pocket exposure if you actually need care.

sections.title: How Age, Household Size, and Tier Move the Number
sections.body: Two people who differ only in age can pay meaningfully different premiums for the identical plan. ACA rules allow insurers to rate premiums by age using a 3:1 curve — a 64-year-old can be charged at most three times what a 21-year-old pays for the same policy, with cost climbing gradually through each age band in between. Household size matters because ACA premiums are typically built by summing per-member costs (with a cap on how many children count toward the total), so adding a spouse or dependent raises the estimated premium roughly in proportion. Plan tier moves the premium in the opposite direction of your expected out-of-pocket costs: Bronze carries the lowest premiums and highest deductibles, Platinum the highest premiums and lowest cost-sharing, with Silver in the middle — and Silver carries the added significance of being the tier subsidies and cost-sharing reductions are benchmarked against. In the real market, insurers also price by rating area (your ZIP code or county) and, in most states, by tobacco use — factors this simplified tool doesn't ask for, so treat the output as a planning range rather than a quote tied to your address.

sections.title: How the Subsidy Estimate Works
sections.body: The estimated subsidy figure approximates the Premium Tax Credit (PTC), the ACA's income-based discount on Marketplace premiums. Eligibility and size of the credit are driven by your household income as a percentage of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL) for your household size, compared against the cost of the benchmark plan — the second-cheapest Silver plan available where you live. As an example: a 40-year-old in a mid-cost-of-living state might see an unsubsidized Silver benchmark premium around $450–$550 a month. If that person is part of a two-person household with income near 250% of the Federal Poverty Level (about $40,880 for a household of two under 2026 guidelines), the ACA's sliding scale would cap their expected contribution toward that benchmark Silver plan at roughly 4% of income — about $136 a month — with the Premium Tax Credit covering the difference. Households under 150% of FPL can see the benchmark plan reduced close to $0; the credit phases down as income rises, and current law removes the old 400%-of-FPL cliff so credits can still apply somewhat above that line, though the details shift with legislation. Because this calculator can't see your ZIP code, exact FPL guideline year, or actual plan menu, treat its subsidy figure as a rough planning estimate, not a real quote — confirm real eligibility and amounts directly at HealthCare.gov or your state Marketplace.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Annual Income
howToSteps.description: Enter your expected annual household income (MAGI) for the coverage year — this is what determines your Premium Tax Credit eligibility, so a realistic figure matters more here than for any other field.

howToSteps.title: Enter Age, Household Size, and Plan Tier
howToSteps.description: Add your age (used for ACA age-rating), the number of people in your household, and the metal tier you're evaluating — Bronze, Silver, Gold, or Platinum. Each of these shifts the estimate independently.

howToSteps.title: Click Calculate
howToSteps.description: Run the numbers to generate an instant estimate — everything happens in your browser, so no application or personal data is submitted anywhere.

howToSteps.title: Review Your Estimated Premium and Subsidy
howToSteps.description: Check the estimated monthly premium, annual premium, and estimated subsidy together. Use them as a starting range, then compare against real plan quotes for your ZIP code during enrollment.

tips: Enter your expected Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) for the coverage year, not last year's income — Marketplace subsidies are based on your estimate for the year you're enrolling.
Try the Silver tier even if you expect to pick Bronze — Silver is the tier subsidy amounts are calculated against, so it's the most useful comparison point.
Run the numbers at your current household size and again with any expected changes, such as a new baby or a dependent aging out, since both income and family size drive the subsidy estimate.
If you or a household member use tobacco, expect your real quote to run higher than this estimate — most states allow tobacco surcharges this simplified tool doesn't model.
Treat the result as a planning range, not a locked-in number — always confirm your actual premium and subsidy through HealthCare.gov, your state exchange, or a licensed agent before enrolling.
